module_title: Collective Responsibility, Anti-Defection, and Presidential Discretion
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the deep systemic doctrines that keep the executive accountable, the legal warfare surrounding defections, and the constitutional limits of the President's power.

core_concepts.title: The Doctrine of Collective Responsibility (Article 75(3))
core_concepts.description:
The bedrock of the parliamentary system. 'The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People (Lok Sabha).'
- Meaning: Ministers swim and sink together. If a No-Confidence Motion is passed in the Lok Sabha against even a single minister or a specific policy, the **entire Council of Ministers must resign**. They cannot claim individual disagreement.

core_concepts.title: Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule)
core_concepts.description:
Added by the 52nd Amendment Act (1985) to prevent 'Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram' politics.
- Disqualification grounds: Voluntarily giving up party membership, or voting contrary to the party whip.
- Exception: If a split involves at least **two-thirds (2/3)** of the legislative party members merging with another party, it is not defection (originally it was 1/3, changed by the 91st Amendment in 2003).
- Deciding Authority: The Presiding Officer (Speaker/Chairman). In *Kihoto Hollohan vs. Zachillhu (1992)*, the Supreme Court ruled that the Speaker's decision is subject to Judicial Review.

core_concepts.title: The President and the Council of Ministers (Articles 74 & 75)
core_concepts.description:
Does the President have real power? 
- 42nd Amendment (1976): Made the advice of the CoM absolutely binding on the President.
- 44th Amendment (1978): Restored a slight balance by allowing the President to send the advice back for reconsideration **once**. If the CoM sends it back again, the President is bound to act on it.
- Situational Discretion: The President exercises true discretion only in 'hung parliaments' (no clear majority) to invite a leader to form the government, or in dismissing a CoM that has lost confidence but refuses to resign.

core_concepts.title: Parliamentary Privileges (Article 105)
core_concepts.description:
Special rights and immunities enjoyed by MPs to discharge their duties effectively.
- Freedom of Speech: An MP cannot be sued or prosecuted for anything said or any vote given in Parliament.
- Freedom from Arrest: An MP cannot be arrested in a **civil case** 40 days before, during, and 40 days after a parliamentary session. (This immunity does NOT apply to criminal cases or preventive detention).

important_entities.name: Doctrine of Pleasure (Article 310)
important_entities.key_fact: Civil servants and ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President.
important_entities.significance: Under Article 75(2), ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President. However, practically, the President can only exercise this 'pleasure' to dismiss a minister on the advice of the Prime Minister.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A highly specific UPSC trap: Does the Anti-Defection law apply to nominated members (like artists/scientists in Rajya Sabha)? Yes, but with a twist. A nominated member is disqualified if they join a political party **after six months** from the date they took their seat. They are allowed to join a party *within* the first six months.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: The 52nd Amendment allowed splits of 1/3rd members. The 91st Amendment made it stricter, requiring a 2/3rd merger to escape disqualification.

exam_strategy_tips: If an advanced Judiciary question asks 'Is the decision of the Speaker under the Tenth Schedule final and immune from court interference?', the answer is **NO**. The Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan established that it is a quasi-judicial function subject to Judicial Review.
